articles.text: Diplomat and legal scholar Jeff Bleich spoke to a packed house at the home of Ellen and Pete Wilson on Wednesday, April 16. The event was organized by the Community Engagement Committee of the Piedmont Education Foundation (PEF). Bleich spoke about the fall in democracy worldwide. His current book updates Machiavelli’s The Prince for modern times. Bleich’s illustrious legal career includes clerking for the Chief Justice of the United States, serving as President of the State Bar of California, and providing special counsel to President Obama. He was the point man in California for Obama’s successful election as U.S. President and served as U.S. Ambassador to Australia, senior advisor to the director of National Intelligence, and chair of the California State University Board of Trustees. His works focus principally on democracy, international relations, and constitutional law. A long time resident of Piedmont, Bleich is currently a fellow at Stanford’s Center for Advanced Study in Behavioral Sciences where he is working on two books. The first is an update of progressive prescriptions from the 2nd industrial revolution in the United States to reform and restore functioning Democracy in America. articles.text: Piedmont Recreation Department’s Play Like a Girl returns this weekend for a free day of hands-on activities, live demonstrations, and inspiring role models – all designed to get girls interested in playing sports. The free event takes place on Sunday, May 4, from 10:00 a.m.-2:00 p.m. at Witter Field. Now in its fourth year, Play Like a Girl invites girls from ages 2-18 throughout the Bay Area to try sports from field hockey to flag football to roller derby with support from skilled athletes and coaches. If a girl wants to continue exploring a sport, there will be information available about classes, leagues, and camps. Play Like a Girl+ 2025 will feature a meeting with former WBNA player Layshia Clarendon and 5-time Olympic swimming gold medalist Dana Vollmer-Grant. Lifelong benefits of sports Participation in sports builds skills that support girls throughout their lives, teaching leadership, discipline, and teamwork. Girls who participate in sports experience lower rates of depression and higher self-esteem than their non-athlete peers. Research has shown a direct link between participation in sports and better educational opportunities, positive health outcomes, and improved career outcomes for girls: • Girls who participate in sports are significantly more likely to graduate high school compared to non-athletes. • Overall, young girls who play sports have higher grades and score higher on standardized tests than non-athletes. • Girls who participate in high school sports have higher rates • of labor force participation and earn 7% higher wages than non-athlete peers. In a 2013 study of 821 senior managers and executives, 94% of female executives reported playing organized sports after primary school. Play Like a Girl+ is made possible by the support of title sponsor Dress Best for Less and many Piedmont athletic organizations hosting stations, including the PHS women’s basketball team, PHS flag football team, Piedmont DEVO mountain biking team, Piedmont junior running club, Piedmont Baseball & Softball Foundation, Piedmont Soccer Club, PMS Sports, Piedmont swim club, and the PHS track & field team. Visit piedmont.ca.gov/PlayLikeAGirl for details, to register, or to sign up to volunteer. A father helps his daughter with a golf swing at last year’s event.

articles.text: City Council study sessions have begun for a walkthrough of the Draft Moraga Canyon Specific Plan, a housing plan that provides space for 199 new housing units in Piedmont. The first study session took place on Monday, April 28, with the next study session taking place tonight, Wednesday, April 30, at 5:30 p.m. at Piedmont High School Library. The aim of these study sessions is to provide a “first look” overview of the recently released Draft Moraga Canyon Specific Plan. Using the big picture vision as a starting point, the April 28 study session focused on the mechanics of implementing the Specific Plan once it’s been adopted. The April 30 meeting will offer a deep dive into the built environment, as defined in the draft document, covering roadway improvements, building design, landscaping, and infrastructure. The study sessions mark the beginning of an extensive public review period and series of meetings before the Council is expected to consider adoption of the Specific Plan next fall. This public review period also includes the following meetings: • June 4, 2025: Park Commission • June 18, 2025: Recreation Commission • August-September 2025: Public hearings at Planning Commission and City Council Community members are encouraged to attend the study sessions. For those unable to join, presentation materials will be available on the project website after the meeting. Multifamily Housing in Moraga Canyon The product of study and community engagement beginning in summer 2023, the Draft Moraga Canyon Specific Plan outlines a vision for a new neighborhood in Moraga Canyon that would: • bring new housing to Piedmont, creating opportunities for people of all income levels • enhance recreational amenities through an expanded sports field and new hiking trail • improve road safety with a new bike lane, sidewalks, and traffic signal at Red Rock Road • model best practices in wildfire resistant construction and landscaping The Draft Specific Plan details development locations, site improvements, and infrastructure requirements for the construction up to 199 units of new housing on City-owned land in Moraga Canyon, 60 of which would be affordable to lower income households. The document anticipates development of multifamily residential buildings between four and six stories and includes two options for where these buildings could be located – either on the north side or the south side of Moraga Avenue. It includes 10 chapters, each one addressing a single topic in detail, with subjects ranging from overall site vision to circulation and traffic safety improvements to building and landscape design. The final chapter outlines an implementation strategy and options for project financing. The Draft Specific Plan is available for download and review at piedmont.ca.gov/MCSP. Submit comments online or by mail Community members can offer comments on the Draft Specific Plan: • online at piedmont.ca.gov/ MCSPComments • by email to MoragaCanyonNews@piedmont.ca.gov • by mail to: Kevin Jackson, Planning & Building Director, 120 Vista Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611 The City Council is expected to consider adoption of the Specific Plan in fall 2025, following a recommendation from the Planning Commission. Learn more about the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan and view video and materials from past meetings and events at piedmont.ca.gov/MCSP.

articles.text: The City of Piedmont is inviting community members to help shape an initiative to develop “objective design standards” for new housing in Piedmont by completing a short online survey. State law now requires cities to approve certain new housing projects, including accessory dwelling units and SB9 applications, based on “objective” standards – those that require no subjective judgement or interpretation by public officials. The Objective Design Standards initiative aims to create clear, measurable, and enforceable rules governing design elements like articulation and massing, providing residents, property owners, and developers clear and consistent expectations for what new housing in Piedmont will look like. This survey is an opportunity for community members to help shape the standards by sharing their preferences and priorities. The survey asks: • How important is architectural consistency within neighborhoods? • What architectural elements are the most important, regardless of style? • How important are building and site features like porches, balconies, low fences, and open front yards? • What would your biggest concerns be if a new home or major addition was built next door to you? The survey should take about 10 minutes to complete and is available at piedmont.ca.gov/ ODSSurvey. Responses will be accepted through May 19. Feedback will help ensure new construction respects the design qualities that residents value most. In Piedmont, objective design standards already exist for accessory dwelling units (ADUs) and multi-family and mixed-use developments. This initiative is developing new objective standards for one-to-four unit residential development and updating the existing standards for other housing types. articles.text: Betty C. Howard Award winners acknowledged at Volunteer Reception City officials and staff applaud City volunteers at the annual Volunteer Appreciation Reception. Piedmont City officials gathered to honor outgoing Commission and Committee volunteers, Betty C. Howard award recipients Gail Lombardi and Carrie Villa, and longtime Police Department volunteer Stanley Silverman at a Volunteer Appreciation event in Piedmont Community Hall last Tuesday, April 22. The event began with an introduction by Mayor Betsy Andersen, followed by a recognition of outgoing Commission and Committee volunteers. “I love looking out and seeing our amazing volunteers,” said Mayor Andersen at the start of the ceremony. “You all give so much to our community. Piedmont would not be the place that it is without your effort and time and love for one another and for our community.” Now in its 46th year, the Betty C. Howard award was created in 1979 by then Recreation Director Mark Delventhal as a way to honor volunteers and staff members for their dedication. articles.text: Dr. Stephen Main, Minister of Music at Piedmont Community Church, is set to have his original cantata, The Image, performed in New York on Wednesday, June 4, at 6:30 p.m. at Trinity Church, Wall Street. Born and raised in New York City, Main studied violin, piano, organ, theory and composition at Oberlin Conservatory, where he received his Bachelor’s Degree of Music in Organ Performance. At the same time, he earned a B.A., M.A., and Ph.D. in Religious Philosophy from the University of Chicago. As a composer, Main’s work includes numerous published choral and orchestral works, regular commissions, and film scores. He has also received the John Ness Beck Award for outstanding achievement in choral composition. Main’s cantata was first unveiled at Piedmont Community Church in June 2023 with choir and full orchestra. Based on an original concept and many conversations with choir member Joe Scherer, Main composed the music and wrote the verse. “The western philosophical and theological idea of the image of God, the imago Dei as it’s called in Latin... has been a foundation for western ideals of democracy,” explained Main about the impetus of his composition. Main’s cantata is now set to play at the historical East Coast venue, Trinity Church on Wall Street. Founded in 1697, this pre-revolutionary church contains the gravesite of Alexander Hamilton. The Image has been added to Trinity Church’s Spring Concert Series, which is free to the public and will be livestreamed internationally. However, in order to fit into this year’s schedule, Piedmont Community Church was asked to pay for the orchestra – a cost of $40,000. “It came to their attention long after they’d already budgeted their year,” explained Main about Trinity Church. “And like a lot of Stephen Main, Music Director and Composer at Piedmont Community Church churches, they write their budgets and then it’s all secured.” Working with Piedmont Community Church, Trinity Church offered to cover the cost of the choir, rehearsals, insurance, technical audio staff, publicity and more in order to fit them into the church’s Concert Series schedule for 2025. Piedmont Community Church has raised more than $18,000 toward the cost of the orchestra as of April 22, and is accepting donations on their website or through mailing a check to the church noting “The Image”. Some church members will be traveling to New York to be at the concert live, and there will be a watch party at the Community Church for the concert. For residents wanting to see Main’s choral and orchestral work in person, Main encourages community members to check out the performance of another one of his pieces, Where Everything is Music. This piece will be performed at the Community Church on June 1, the Sunday right before Main flies to New York to help Trinity Church with The Image. “What I’m hoping happens from ‘The Image’ is that I would love it to redound to the glory of Piedmont,” said Main. “because I really believe in Piedmont Church and I’m very proud of my musicians.”

articles.text: May can be a challenging month for students. Endurance to get through the school year is flagging, yet there are still significant hurdles to overcome before the promise of summer arrives. Whether you have a student taking AP exams, facing looming finals, or exhibiting a raging case of Senioritis (regardless of their age), here are some strategies for parents to help manage May stress. Communication is key Anyone with school-aged kids can relate to the idea that “May is the new December.” May is the month of dance recitals, band concerts, end-of-season sports banquets, and more. While it is fun to celebrate the hard work of our kids and their classmates, it can be exhausting. Taking some time now to read the backlog of emails and mark the important dates on your calendar can help avoid last-minute scheduling disappointment. Having a conversation with your high schooler now about time management in May will allow you both to identify issues while there is still time to resolve them. Ask your student to tell you about their plans for preparing for tests and finals. Remind them that even though we’re nearing crunch time, there is still time to schedule help with the teacher or an academic tutor. If there are family obligations during May that include your teen, let them know as soon as possible. Show your support Both AP tests and finals feel very high stakes to students. If your schedule allows, offering a healthy breakfast or a ride to school could help your student feel supported on a really stressful day. These simple gestures can help calm a stimulated amygdala and allow your student’s brain to focus rather than be derailed by testing stress. Students who are finishing 8th or 12th grade may be anxious about their transition to high school or college. Acknowledging that these feelings are valid goes a long way to helping your child feel better about the uncertainty of change. The end of the school year is always filled with big emotions. Here’s to getting through May with as much joy and as little stress as possible! Karen Shopoff Rooff is Director of College Consulting at Study Smarter. Study Smarter has been providing individualized academic tutoring, test preparation, and college counseling to Piedmont families since 1997. Karen is a former college professor and an experienced coach. For more information please visit www. studysmarter.com, email info@ studysmarter.com, or call (510) 350-8444.

Managing school stress during May By Karen Shopoff Rooff May can be a challenging month for students. Endurance to get through the school year is flagging, yet there are still significant hurdles to overcome before the promise of summer arrives. Whether you have a student taking AP exams, facing looming finals, or exhibiting a raging case of Senioritis (regardless of their age), here are some strategies for parents to help manage May stress. Communication is key Anyone with school-aged kids can relate to the idea that “May is the new December.” May is the month of dance recitals, band concerts, end-of-season sports banquets, and more. While it is fun to celebrate the hard work of our kids and their classmates, it can be exhausting. Taking some time now to read the backlog of emails and mark the important dates on your calendar can help avoid last-minute scheduling disappointment. Having a conversation with your high schooler now about time management in May will allow you both to identify issues while there is still time to resolve them. Ask your student to tell you about their plans for preparing for tests and finals. Remind them that even though we’re nearing crunch time, there is still time to schedule help with the teacher or an academic tutor. If there are family obligations during May that include your teen, let them know as soon as possible. Show your support Both AP tests and finals feel very high stakes to students. If your schedule allows, offering a healthy breakfast or a ride to school could help your student feel supported on a really stressful day. These simple gestures can help calm a stimulated amygdala and allow your student’s brain to focus rather than be derailed by testing stress. Students who are finishing 8th or 12th grade may be anxious about their transition to high school or college. Acknowledging that these feelings are valid goes a long way to helping your child feel better about the uncertainty of change. The end of the school year is always filled with big emotions. Here’s to getting through May with as much joy and as little stress as possible! Karen Shopoff Rooff is Director of College Consulting at Study Smarter. articles.text: Wildwood fourth graders piled aboard a school bus in the early morning of April 17 for a field trip to Sacramento. Once in the state’s capitol, classes split up to take a tour of the Capitol before coming back for a self-guided scavenger hunt at Sutter’s Fort. Parent chaperones drove in separate cars and met the bus full of fourth graders and teachers at the West Entrance of the Capitol. It was students’ first school field trip on a bus. Jennifer Kessler’s class went into the building to take the tour while Martin Lewis’ class made sketches of the building. Sketchers noted the number of columns, windows and Minerva, the Roman goddess of wisdom, justice and law, in their drawings. While on the tour, they learned that there was supposed to be a grand staircase entrance on the west side, but it was never completed leaving visitors a grand portico instead. “I felt so immersed in the history of the capitol building. Our docent did a tremendous job of presenting fun, enticing and captivating facts as he took all of our students through the Treasury room, the main hallways with the detailed paintings of past governors, as well as the details of the chamber. The tour flew by because of how interactive it was,” said parent chaperone Jess Nisenbaum. After the tour, the fourth graders gathered together for a photo in front of the Capitol and then hopped back on the bus to drive to Sutter’s Fort State Park, where they ate lunch on the lawn, played card games, infection tag, chess and jumped rope. At Sutter’s Fort the fourth graders divided into small groups to find items on their scavenger hunt lists and write down what they noticed about each item. Some areas they visited included the blacksmith shop, the doctor’s office and the weaving room. Many of the spaces provided services and goods for the travelers who had Sutter’s Fort as their final destination on the California trail. The fourth graders ended their long day of learning about California history with a bus ride home and arrived back at Wildwood School around 4:00 p.m. Ayla Martinez (left) and Vera Kriss stand in front of the west entrance of the Capitol. Connor Tornatore sketches the Capitol. Martin Lewis and his 4th grade students in the Treasury room learn about historic vaults at the State Capitol. A tour guide talks about Governor Jerry Brown’s portrait at the State Capitol. Students learn about how representatives vote in the House of Representatives.

John Cullom, the son of Jim “Truck” Cullom, spoke on his father’s behalf. “Truck” was a Class of 1942 graduate and a legendary football star. The Piedmont Sports Hall of Fame inducted six former athletes and two teams on Saturday, April 26 at PHS’ Alan Harvey Theater, marking the first year they’ve entered two full teams. Inductees included Courtney Gault Azad from the Class of 1999 (basketball, softball, tennis), Jim “Truck” Cullom of the Class of 1942 (football), Robby Inch from the Class of 2010 (football, lacrosse), Catey McCreary from the Class of 1983 (basketball, softball), Casey Morris from the Class of 2008 (basketball), and Lauren Remer of the Class of 2013 (soccer, track). Teams inducted featured the 2003-2004 and 2004- 2005 girls’ basketball teams, and the 1976 football team. Founded in 2003 by the late Ken Rawlings and Pete Anderson, and led for many years by former PHS basketball coach Chris Lavdiotis, the Piedmont Sports Hall of Fame honors athletes, coaches, administrators, and community members for outstanding contributions to Piedmont High School athletics. • Courtney Gault Azad, Class of 1999 Honors for Gault started the induction ceremony. A member of the Class of 1999, Gault was a three-sport athlete in tennis, softball and basketball at Piedmont High. She was a four-time All-League recipient in softball and two-time recipient in Basketball. As a pitcher, she threw four no-hitters during her four years as a varsity starter. Gault was introduced by former teammate Julie Skaff. “She deserves this honor both because of her athletic accomplishments and her positive impact on the community,” Skaff said. As a senior, Gault led the softball team to the Division 2A East Bay NCS Championship game, where they fell 7-3 to Dublin. In basketball, she averaged a double-double. Gault went on to attend UCLA and worked in their Athletic Department as a recruiter from her sophomore to senior year. “My teammates were synonymous with my best high school memories. Not just the wins, but even the losses created lifelong friendships,” Gault said. • Jim “Truck” Cullom, Class of 1942 Cullom was a two-year starter on Piedmont High’s legendary football teams, which finished ranked No. 1 in the United States in 1941 and No. 2 the previous year in 1940. He left school early to enlist in World War 2 with the Marine Corps and returned to play football and rugby for the University of California, taking his storied career to the NFL’s Washington Commanders and the New York Yanks. Accepting on the behalf of “Truck” was his son, John Collum, a longtime coach of the PITS rugby team. “My dad loved Piedmont. There was never a question in his or my mom’s mind that they were going to raise their family in Piedmont. My dad, more than anything else, was loyal. He was always loyal to his family, friends, Piedmont and Cal,” John Collum said. On the gridiron, Collum was on the offensive line on Cal’s historic teams under coach Lynn (Pappy) Waldorf from 1947-1949, appearing in two Rose Bowls. His teams were famously known as, “Pappy‘s Boys”. He later re-enlisted to the Marine Corps to serve in the Korean War and returned to Cal as an assistant coach for their rugby team. “Truck” was inducted into the Cal Athletics Hall of Fame in 1995. • Robby Inch, Class of 2010 Inch was a two-sport athlete in football and lacrosse. He was a three-year varsity letterman in lacrosse and played two years of varsity football. He was introduced by former lacrosse coach Jerem Stothers. “He was a great teammate and excelled in both football and lacrosse. He was unstoppable one-on-one to the cage and always looked like a running back running down field. He was guarded by the top defender on every team. If they didn’t, it was over for them. But if they did, it was still over,” Stothers said. As a senior, Inch earned USA Lacrosse High School All American honors, was named the Bay Shore Athletic League MVP, and set a single-season for points scored with 67 goals and 39 assists. PHS went 14-8 in 2010 and reach the NCS Quarterfinals. He also led the football team in touchdowns as a junior and senior. He continued his lacrosse career at Santa Clara University, playing all four years. He went on to complete his MBA degree at Columbia University in 2020. “In sixth grade, I became obsessed with lacrosse. I had amazing teammates, like our goalie Connor Sweeney, who would join me at Witter Field to ‘practice.’ He basically stood in the goal and I would hurl lacrosse balls at him,” Inch said with a laugh. • Catey McCreary, Class of 1983 McCreary was a trend-setter in the Piedmont athletic commuCatey McCreary, Class of 1983, was a trendsetter for early women’s sports at PHS. She played softball and basketball. Casey Morris, Class of 2008, was a member of Piedmont 2004-2005 state title and helped win three NCS titles. nity. She was a four-year varsity starter in both softball and basketball. She was introduced by close friend and former Piedmont City Administrator Sara Lillevand. “Thank you to the committee for honoring our trailblazers. Catey pushed boundaries and changed minds; not because she was a rebel looking for a cause, but simply because she loved to play and compete,” Lillevand said. A standout softball player, McCreary was a four-year starter, earning All-League honors twice and an honorable mention once. She was a three-year varsity athlete in basketball as well, receiving an honorable mention as a junior and All-League as a senior. She continued her athletic career at Cal Poly where she played softball during her freshman year. “We stand on the shoulders of others. For me, that was Julie and Lucy Dickenson, they taught me their love of sports and who Kareem Abdul Jabar was. Betty Richter fired balls so hard at me as a third grader, she prepped me well,” McCreary said. • Casey Morris, Class of 2008 Morris was a four-year starter on Piedmont’s girls’ basketball team from 2004-2008 and was a member of PHS’ storied State title run in 2005 as a freshman. She was introduced by her sister Cheri Morris and joins the Hall of Fame alongside her older sister, Chazny Morris. “I’m pretty sure Casey went straight from crawling to running pick-and-rolls. Growing up, I wanted to be just like her and I copied everything she did. Being like Casey was the ultimate goal,” younger sister Cheri Morris said. As a freshman, Morris was named to Cal-Hi Sports’ all-freshman team and earned third-team all-state honors. She helped lead Piedmont to its third straight NCS title in 2006 as a sophomore, and averaged 24 points per game as a junior towards PHS’ fourth consecutive NCS title. She was named co-MVP of the Bay Shore Athletic League her senior year and earned the San Francisco Chronicle’s all-metro second-team honors. Lauren Remer, Class of 2013, still holds the school’s records in the 200 and 400 meter runs. She continued her playing career at Texas Tech after transferring from Cal, finishing her college at with 1,056 points in three seasons. “I’m extremely grateful to my family, I can talk for ours about my dad and my basketball journey. He deserves all the credit for who I was as a player and who I became after sports,” Casey Morris said. • Lauren Remer, Class of 2013 Remer was a standout athlete in both soccer and track. She still holds school records in the 400 meters with a time of 56.79 set in 2012 and 200 meters in 26.16 set as a senior in 2013. She was introduced by her husband, Cormac Craigie, a PHS alum. “I couldn’t be more proud of you. Back in High School, she used to beat the boys. articles.text: Piedmont High School’s swim team capped off its dual meet season on Friday, April 25 with a spirited performance, as the boys’ varsity team secured a 92-78 victory over Castro Valley while the girls’ varsity team narrowly fell, 84-82 . Despite mixed results in the pool, the evening was a resounding success as the team came together to honor its seniors. “Our biggest highlight was having so much of our team there to celebrate our seniors in their last-ever high school dual meet,” said head coach Adrien Downey. “They put a lot of work into creating posters and sending them off in style. Despite being at another team’s pool, we made it feel like home for a few minutes under the banners and balloons.” The Junior Varsity squads continued their strong season with standout performances. Rabia Mahmood impressed once again, showcasing her versatility with an expanding lineup of events. Rylan Patty delivered exceptional relay splits, and Elles Krieckhaus turned heads by winning the 50-yard butterfly and 500-yard freestyle back-to-back – events he doesn’t typically compete in. “JV’s performances were solid up and down the lineup,” Downey said. “But more than anything, their attitude and enthusiasm, especially during the relays, really stood out.” Overall the night was a meaningful one. Family, friends, and teammates filled the deck with cheers, hugs, and gratitude for the seniors who have been the heart of the program for years. Next, Piedmont heads to the West Alameda County Conference (WACC) Championships, where the stakes will be even higher. The meet will crown team champions for both girls and boys and offer a pathway to postseason competition, including the North Coast Section (NCS) Championships and the State Championships. “It’s a true all-hands-on-deck moment for us,” Downey said. “Depth becomes even more important, and it opens opportunities for our entire roster to contribute to the outcome. We’re excited for what’s ahead.” Piedmont honored its nine seniors on the roster for Senior Night. Pictured are Coach Adrien Downey, Julia Montes, Sonja ten Grotenhuis, Evan Byun, Owen Blanford, Simon March-Cunningham, Inaya Majid, Anna Caputo, Tyler Dacanay, Leo Hurwitz, and Principal David Yoshihara.

articles.text: Berkeley Playhouse will close out its 2024-25 season with The Sound of Music, premiering May 23 and running through June 29. The production, directed by Danny Cozart, is fun for all ages and provides a story of both hope and resistance, with a collection of favorite songs like “My Favorite Things,” “Do-Re-Mi,” and “Sixteen Going on Seventeen.” The musical, based on the 1949 memoir The Story of the Trapp Family Singers, premiered years before the widely-popular 1965 American musical drama film The Sound of Music, produced and directed by Robert Wise. The Sound of Music opened on Broadway at the Lunt-Fontanne Theatre on November 16, 1959, with music by Richard Rodgers and lyrics by Oscar Hammerstein II. Cozart said the beloved, timeless musical is one of his alltime favorites that “continues to become more relevant day by day.” “The themes we are looking to explore in this production are the choices a person must make when the different structures of society [including] family, religion, and the state, are imposing conflicting demands on them.” Cozart said. “Our focus for this production is to drive home the real-world consequences of political action and the impact on a family trying to stay together in the face of looming tyranny.” In addition, the show delves into themes of loss, found family, reconnection, and emotional presence, he added. Cast includes Marah Sotelo as Maria Rainer, Teressa Foss as Mother Abbess, Chloe Angst as Sister Berthe, Sage Alberto as Sister Margaretta, Akshaya Lakshmi as Sister Sophia, Robert Lopez as Captain Georg Von Trapp and Phillip Leyva as Franz. A cast of young musicians will perform the musical’s key songs. To purchase tickets, call the box office at (510) 845-8542 (extension 351) or visit www. berkeleyplayhouse.org. Showtimes vary. Marah Sotelo is Maria Rainer in Berkeley Playhouse’s production The Sound of Music, premiering May 23.

articles.text: Randall Museum, a children’s arts, science and nature museum in San Francisco, has an extensive list of free workshops next month designed for kids of all ages from toddlers to teenagers. The museum is operated by the San Francisco Recreation and Park Department and offers free admission while providing high-quality science and art classes moderated by museum staff, San Francisco Rec and Park employees and various resident natural scientists and zoologists at a low cost. below. May 3 - Cross Stitch Workshop Randall Museum’s science and nature program coordinator Katherine Galeas Veliz moderates a cross stitching workshop ideal for ages 12 and up on Saturday, May 3, from 10 a.m. to 12 p.m. Galeas Veliz will share her love and knowledge of the art of cross stitching and guide young participants through completing a simple stitch design. All levels of skill are welcome and beginners with no cross stitch experience are encouraged to participate. The class is designed to teach the basics of cross stitching and participants are invited to take home their completed project. All materials are included with $25 workshop admission. May 10 & 17 - Threadless Pine Needle Basketry Children aged 11 and up can visit Randall Museum May 10 and 17 for a two-day workshop to learn techniques for coiling, at Corona Heights, searching for San Francisco’s diverse avian creatures. Participants are encouraged to bring their own binoculars on this two-hour excursion, geared for beginning to intermediate birders, in order to catch a glimpse of several habitats on the museum’s campus, each of which is enjoyed by different bird species. Meet in the Randall Museum’s Parking Lot at 199 Museum Way in San Francisco at 8 a.m. on Saturday, May 17, to join the flock. Every Saturday in May - Meet the Animals In addition to a rotating list of art and science workshops, the museum also offers popular yearround exhibits open to the public throughout the week. The Museum’s live animal exhibit, Wild in California, offers an up-close glimpse of California’s natural wildlife. Resident animals at Randall Museum include Lyra the raccoon, who was born with several health problems including deformities of the spine and jaw, and a longtailed weasel named Scarlet who was neglected and sustained injuries while in captivity. Lyra and Scarlet have been rehabilitated by staff and are now animal ambassadors for the museum. At 11:30 a.m. every Saturday in May, visitors can join an open discussion about the museum’s wildlife ambassadors and learn more about resident creatures and the staff who care for them. Visitors of all ages will have the opportunity to meet some of the animals up-close and are encouraged to ask questions to learn more about California’s native wildlife. Participants will also learn about the cultural and historical significance of pine needle basketry at this two-day immersive workshop that’s perfect for middle school aged children. Both workshops begin at 12 p.m. Cost is $65 per person for both workshops which includes all materials. articles.text: A large-scale exhibition featuring digital artwork by Yuan Goang-Ming, one of the foremost Taiwanese artists active in the international media art scene, is on view at the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco now through July 7. Goang-Ming is considered a pioneer of video art in Taiwan and has worked with the digital art medium since 1984. He received the Hsiung-Shih Art Award for the Best New Artist for his video and sculptural work Out of Position (1987) when he was still in art school in 1988. He went on to receive a master’s degree in media art from the Academy of Design, Karlsruhe Germany in 1997 and has exhibited internationally across Asia, Europe, and America since. The Asian Art Museum exhibition Yuan Goang-Ming: Everyday War features numerous works that debuted in GoangMing’s critically acclaimed exhibition representing Taiwan at the 60th Venice Biennale. The largescale exhibition is displayed in the museum’s Akiko Yamazaki and Jerry Yang Pavilion and is the artist’s first North American solo show. “The generational anxiety of this artist known as the ‘father of Taiwanese video art’ offers a timely message,” said Abby Chen, curator of contemporary art at the Asian Art Museum. “As Yuan strives to locate a sense of home and belonging, his visions of an unstable world convey a relatable yearning for safety and peace.” A free docent-led tour of Yuan Goang-Ming: Everyday War will Yuan Goang-Ming be held tomorrow, Thursday, May 1, at 5 p.m. No advance reservation is needed. To join the tour, meet at the exhibition entrance on the ground floor at 5 p.m. Admission to Yuan Goang-Ming: Everyday War is required. To learn more, visit https:// exhibitions.asianart.org/exhibitions/everyday-war/. Photo courtesy of Asian Art Museum Everyday War, 2024, by Yuan Goang-Ming (b. Taipei, 1965). articles.text: 1883 (Season 1), is an extraordinary, richly produced episodic origin series that is, from the opening introductory scenes, relentlessly engaging, wonderfully cast and superbly acted, the writing and the photography inspired. We soon come to realize that episodic storytelling can transcend the familiar two-hour cinema format, which has, for more than a century, defined the movie-going experience. The series is set during those early post-civil war years when the nation and its denizens are just beginning to recover from the trauma and loss of what was a lethal and divisive Civil War. The opening scene is of a man, Shea Brennan (Sam Elliot), sitting alone on the porch of his farmhouse, lost in grief. He goes inside, carries his lifeless daughter (small pox we assume) upstairs, places her on a bed next to her deceased mother, and grimly returns to the front of the house and throws a kerosene lamp through a window. He stands back watching all that he cares about consumed by fire. The narrative then cuts to Ft. Worth, Texas, 1883, referred to as “Hell’s Half Acre,” the wide dirt street, bordered by stores, a saloon, is teeming with hardscrabble people, wagons, horses, all seeming on the verge of chaos and lawlessness. It’s there that we’re introduced to James Dutton (Tim McGraw), arriving alone in Ft. Worth in a covered wagon. His appearance is frayed, heavily bearded, well armed, clearly not intimidated by what he sees. He’s in Ft. Worth to await the arrival of his wife, Margaret (Faith Hill), teenage daughter, Elsa (Isabel May), and young son, John (Rick Audie), arriving by train from Tennessee. We soon learn that the Dutton family intends to travel by wagon West in search of land and a new life. Circumstances lead to James meeting Shea (aka Captain, his rank in the Union Army), and reluctantly agrees to travel with but not join Shea’s wagon train, comprised of Slavic and German immigrants, their wagons laden with all that they possess, and incapable of understanding what the journey before them will entail. At their core all they know is that they will never, no matter the cost, return to the repression Gratiela Brancusi, Sam Elliott and LaMonica Garrett in 1883

articles.text: Pom Poko is an unusual film perhaps best suited for older tweens, teens, and adults. Its audience may be those who find pleasure in taking a deep dive into the extraordinary work that has, for decades, been the signature of Studio Ghibli. The hand-drawn animation of Pom Poko is remarkable, wrapped in wonderfully imagined moments. If there is a weakness it resides in the storytelling. First, you should know that the words Pom Poko refer to what are called, in Japanese mythology, tanuki, or “raccoon dogs”. They look like a cross between a raccoon and a wolverine, thought to be as amiable as a hedgehog, with huge pouches (aka testicles). These raccoons are said to be mischievous and capable of using the “illusion science” of shape-shifting in which they can transform themselves into anthropomorphic animals). The story begins in 1960 when the habitat of the tanuki is threatened by a giant subdivision, called Tama Hills, on the outskirts of Tokyo, causing distress for not only the forest wildlife, but most especially the tanuki. The story resumes in 1990 when the tanuki matriarch, Oroku (Tess MacNeille), plus the warlike chief, Gonta (Clancy Brown), and the resourceful Shoukichi (Jonathan Taylor Thomas) urge the tribe to resist the expanding encroachment. And so begins the confrontation between the tanuki and the developers, realistic and cartoonish, occasionally spiced up with trickery, as when some tanuki go undercover, shape-shifting to appear human while roaming the urban streets. The threads that stich the narrative together, both melodramatic and cartoonish, are numerous but often lack focus, and are, on occasion, leavened by slapstick. At one point, a pageant of mystical creatures are on parade, as well as a huge tsunami, both intended to scare the construction crews and the townies. This tanuki strategy also includes construction-site sabotage that does frighten and even kills some of the workers. Much of Pom Poko is surreal, at times manic, relying on the sustained attempt by the tanuki to terrorize the humans. Pom Poko. Directed by Isao Takahata. Animé from Studio Ghibli. With the voices of Jonathan Taylor Thomas, Clancy Brown, Tess MacNeille and Andre Stojka. 1 hr., 52 min. Rated PG. Released in 1994. Streaming on prime/MAX/apple tv/Fandango. articles.text: Ewan McGregor in Christopher Robin Christopher Robin is a live-action/animated fantasy film inspired by the books of A.A. Milne, replete with the iconic illustrations of E.H. Shepard. If I had to select an ideal age for this movie I would pick older kids and tweens, despite the strong animated opening. The tale begins with a young Christopher Robin in 100 Acre Woods with his friends Winnie the Pooh, Piglet, Tigger et.al. The lad is about to leave for boarding school, and the gang is giving him a farewell tea party. Christopher comforts Winnie (Jim Cummings), reassuring the honey-loving bear that he will never forget him. And so begins the transition from animation to live-action. As it turns out, the boy has a difficult time in school, his father unexpectedly dies, and he soon puts the 100 Acre Woods behind him. He grows up (now played by Ewan McGregor), marries an architect, Evelyn (Hayley Atwell), has a daughter, Madeline (Bronte Carmichael), and serves in WWII. After the war, he finds a demanding job with Winslow Luggage Co. as an efficiency expert, working long hours while increasingly neglecting his family. In other words, Christopher is losing perspective, putting his work before everything else, including a promised family vacation. This commitment to his job takes the story to that one day when Christopher is sitting on a bench in London’s Langdon

articles.text: New York Life Insurance Company and New York Life Insurance and Annuity Corporation The first image that often comes to mind when people think about long-term care is an elderly person sitting alone in a depressing nursing home. The misconceptions about what longterm care involves and peoples’ images of the most common care settings are understandable, since long-term care insurance originally started as nursing home insurance four decades ago. However, it has evolved into a much more flexible solution that allows you to receive care in a variety of settings. Most of us want the ability to age at home, in a familiar setting surrounded by family and our favorite things. The fact is, 90 percent of adults who need long-term care services receive assistance at home or in another community setting.1 If the level of care you need evolves over time, most longterm care insurance policies not only allow you to transition to a nursing home, but some may also provide you with support during the transition. Since you can’t predict the care you might eventually need, it’s important to have the flexibility to choose the setting that best fits your needs at any given time. Many long-term care policies available today can provide you with a choice of where you want to receive care, including: • At home, with the help of a home health aide or in some cases a family member or friend to assist with daily activities • In a community setting, such as adult day care services • At an assisted living facility, where you can receive help with transportation and meals • In a nursing home, if you need around-the-clock care Each of these options provides a different level of care depending on how much assistance you need. Receiving care at home is the most popular and preferred option, and some policies even provide benefits that allow you to make home modifications that can help you stay at home longer. Policies that provide home care allow you to receive care from a professional, or possibly a friend or family member if informal care is covered. While most people hope they won’t ever need to worry about long-term care, the reality is Americans have almost a 70 percent chance they will need some type of long-term care assistance after age 65.2 Women are even more at risk, primarily because they tend to live longer. The thought of not being able to care for yourself can be difficult and creating a strategy for care can be daunting. However, it’s best to not let long-term care preparation get pushed aside, because your age and health both factor into whether you’ll qualify for insurance and how much you’ll pay for coverage. have the peace of mind that you’ve taken the steps to help protect your family from the financial and emotional impact of a long-term care event. Take the time to research available options, decide how much coverage you need based on estimated costs, and create a strategy that will give you the flexibility to choose where and how you receive care. pages.text: 26 26 Wednesday, April 30, 2025 Computer tips and helpful suggestions, especially for people who are not entirely comfortable using their computers. By Cookie Segelstein Dear MacMama, I’m about to get a new laptop, and I want to get all the information from my old Mac to the new. Is it something that I can do myself? Or is it something that I need professional help to do? I’m pretty savvy with technology, but I’m no expert. Goeff, Piedmont Dear Geoff, If you’re feeling up to it, you can absolutely set up your new Mac yourself—and if you run into trouble, AppleCare can walk you through it at 1-800-275-2273. I’ll explain one of the easiest ways: using Migration Assistant. First, place your old Mac and your new Mac next to each other. Make sure the old Mac is powered on, connected to Wi-Fi, and ideally plugged into a power source. Then, turn on the new Mac. As you go through the setup assistant, you’ll choose your language, your country, and either enable or skip accessibility options. You’ll connect to your Wi-Fi network, enter the password, and accept Apple’s privacy notice. Soon, you’ll reach a screen asking if you want to transfer information to this Mac. Choose the option to transfer from a Mac, Time Machine backup, or startup disk. Now it’s time to open Migration Assistant on your old Mac. You’ll find it in the Applications folder, inside the Utilities folder. Open it, click Continue, and enter your computer login password (the one you use for downloads, not your Apple ID password). Then select “Transfer to another Mac.” If you have a Thunderbolt cable—and the right adapter if needed—you can connect the two machines directly, which will make the process much faster. If not, using Wi-Fi works too, although it will be slower. On your new Mac, you should soon see your old Mac appear. Select it. A six-digit code will show up on both screens; check that they match and click to confirm. You’ll then see a list of information you can transfer, such as your applications, documents, and settings. In most cases, you’ll want to leave everything selected. Click Continue, and the migration will begin. If you have non-Apple software, you’ll need to re-enter your login information afterward (e.g., Microsoft Office, Adobe Creative Cloud). You may also need to re-enter your email passwords. The transfer can take anywhere from a couple of hours to most of the day, depending on how much data you have and whether you are using a cable or Wi-Fi. Once it’s finished, your new Mac should look and feel a lot like your old one. If you are transferring from a Time Machine backup instead, the process is very similar. Plug in the backup drive when prompted, and Migration Assistant will recognize it and guide you through selecting the most recent backup. Some people prefer to skip transferring everything and set up their Mac fresh, especially if their old computer had glitches or other issues. If you use iCloud, you can easily restore your contacts, calendars, photos, documents, passwords, and bookmarks by signing in with your Apple ID. You would then need to manually reinstall any non-Apple software, like Microsoft Office, Chrome, or Zoom. This method gives you a clean start, although you will need to manually move over anything not stored in iCloud, such as a music library. Each approach has its pros and cons. If something goes wrong during the migration, you can restart and try again. Long-term care insurance offers more than just nursing home coverage New York Life Insurance Company and New York Life Insurance and Annuity Corporation The first image that often comes to mind when people think about long-term care is an elderly person sitting alone in a depressing nursing home. The misconceptions about what longterm care involves and peoples’ images of the most common care settings are understandable, since long-term care insurance originally started as nursing home insurance four decades ago. However, it has evolved into a much more flexible solution that allows you to receive care in a variety of settings. Most of us want the ability to age at home, in a familiar setting surrounded by family and our favorite things. The fact is, 90 percent of adults who need long-term care services receive assistance at home or in another community setting.1 If the level of care you need evolves over time, most longterm care insurance policies not only allow you to transition to a nursing home, but some may also provide you with support during the transition. Since you can’t predict the care you might eventually need, it’s important to have the flexibility to choose the setting that best fits your needs at any given time. Many long-term care policies available today can provide you with a choice of where you want to receive care, including: • At home, with the help of a home health aide or in some cases a family member or friend to assist with daily activities • In a community setting, such as adult day care services • At an assisted living facility, where you can receive help with transportation and meals • In a nursing home, if you need around-the-clock care Each of these options provides a different level of care depending on how much assistance you need. Receiving care at home is the most popular and preferred option, and some policies even provide benefits that allow you to make home modifications that can help you stay at home longer. Policies that provide home care allow you to receive care from a professional, or possibly a friend or family member if informal care is covered. While most people hope they won’t ever need to worry about long-term care, the reality is Americans have almost a 70 percent chance they will need some type of long-term care assistance after age 65.2 Women are even more at risk, primarily because they tend to live longer. The thought of not being able to care for yourself can be difficult and creating a strategy for care can be daunting. However, it’s best to not let long-term care preparation get pushed aside, because your age and health both factor into whether you’ll qualify for insurance and how much you’ll pay for coverage. By including long-term care in your retirement strategy, you’ll have the peace of mind that you’ve taken the steps to help protect your family from the financial and emotional impact of a long-term care event. Take the time to research available options, decide how much coverage you need based on estimated costs, and create a strategy that will give you the flexibility to choose where and how you receive care. In recent years more focus has been placed on fostering a community of sustainability. “We will plant a tree,” assured Parks and Project Manager Nancy Kent about the City’s annual Arbor Day traditions. “Recently it’s been more related to getting the community together, having sustainability, having our big trucks so people can see what Public Works does, and then the whole leaf blower thing was to try and get people to understand that you don’t want to be using gas blowers in the city.” Owls receive Official Names The City’s naming contest came to a close at the celebration, with the winning submission by former Piedmont Post reporter Allyson Aleksey, a new resident of Piedmont. The winning names are Ramona and Blair. The pair of great horned owls will continue nesting in Dracena Park.
